question: A 23-year-old man presents to an outpatient psychiatrist complaining of anxiety and a persistent feeling that “something terrible will happen to my family.” He describes 1 year of vague, disturbing thoughts about his family members contracting a “horrible disease” or dying in an accident. He believes that he can prevent these outcomes by washing his hands of “the contaminants” any time that he touches something and by performing praying and counting rituals each time that he has unwanted, disturbing thoughts. The thoughts and rituals have become more frequent recently, making it impossible for him to work, and he expresses feeling deeply embarrassed by them. Which of the following is the most effective treatment for this patient's disorder?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) -> intrusive, unwanted thoughts -> compulsive behaviors (handwashing, praying, counting) -> functional impairment -> cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) -> symptom reduction -> improved quality of life -> 90%

CHAIN: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) -> serotonin dysregulation -> selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like fluoxetine -> symptom improvement -> cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) -> enhanced treatment response -> 85%
enhanced_information: For the treatment of this patient's disorder characterized by intrusive, unwanted thoughts and compulsive behaviors leading to functional impairment, the most effective approach is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) combined with fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). Consensus supports the use of SSRIs like fluoxetine in OCD to improve symptoms, which can enhance the response to CBT, leading to symptom reduction and improved quality of life.
analysis: The core medical principle for the treatment of this patient's disorder, likely obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), involves a combination of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and pharmacotherapy. Consensus and enhanced information support the use of SSRIs like fluoxetine in OCD to improve symptoms, which can enhance the response to CBT. Clonazepam and haloperidol are not first-line treatments for OCD. Psychodynamic psychotherapy alone is not the recommended approach for OCD. Aripiprazole is not the first-line pharmacological choice for OCD. Therefore, the most likely correct option is cognitive behavioral therapy and fluoxetine.
